task_prompt: Is it important to care about climate change?
response_text:
It is essential that we do everything we can to combat climate change. Climate change is affecting our everyday lives, leaving immense impacts on the environment. It's causing animal species to disappear, water bodies to become polluted, and the ozone layer to break down.

To be able to fight back against climate change, we first need to understand what it is and what causes it. Climate change is the change in the earth's temperature, caused by the release of greenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide and methane, into the atmosphere. This causes the atmosphere to warm up, making its temperatures increase. One of the main factors of the climate is the ocean. When the atmosphere heats up, glaciers in the ocean melt, causing the sea levels to rise. Some species of plants and animals are not used to being in warmer temperatures. The rise in temperature can cause these species to become endangered, which is what is happening with the polar bear. One species population  decreasing can cause many problems down the food chain, putting other species in danger. One everyday activity that can cause climate change is driving gas-powered cars. When these cars run they burn gas, emitting carbon monoxide, a greenhouse gas. Some of the main causes of climate change are industrial activities. In factories, many fuels are burned to create energy, leading to large amounts of CO2 emissions every single day. Factories tend to have poor waste management, dumping their toxic chemicals into the ocean. This can pollute water bodies, making them a dangerous and unsafe habitat for the species living there. Another common industrial activity is deforestation, which is the process of cutting down trees for the purpose of harvesting lumber. Trees are a major factor in preventing climate change, as they take in carbon dioxide, a major greenhouse gas, and emit it as oxygen.

Now that we understand climate change and its causes, it's time to understand how we can prevent it from happening. Firstly, at an individual level we can stop littering, use electric vehicles, and use public transport/carpooling to cut down on carbon emissions. As a society, we can cut down on industrial activities such as burning coal, and use other energy sources such as solar energy or hydro-electricity. In factories, we can implement proper waste disposal practices and techniques. To combat deforestation, we should reduce the amount of trees we cut down and try to plant at least double or triple the trees removed.

In conclusion, it is important that we do everything we can to fight back against climate change to save our planet. To do this, we can reduce industrial activites such as deforestation and cut down on carbon emissions from vehicles. It's important that we give our best efforts to save the environment to ensure that life on earth will prosper for many years to come.

task_prompt: Would you live in a place that is always warm?
response_text:
I would not live in a place that is always warm. While warm weather brings sunshine, sunflowers, and human-friendly temperatures, it has some cons. The constant warm weather would not allow me to experience different climates, lack a diverse ecosystem, and cause a rise in health concerns. 

One reason I would not want to live in a place that is always warm is because the warm weather would only allow me to experience the summer climate. I want to enjoy other seasons as well such as winter and fall. The activities that come with these seasons are not something I want to miss. I enjoy snowboarding and staying indoors during cold weather. However, I would be unable to participate in these activities because of the constant warm climate in the area. 

Another reason I would not live in a constantly warm place is due to the lack of diversity because of the lack of different seasons. When there will not be other seasons that introduce cold weather, the ecosystem in the area would change. There would be little to no rain in order to grow and provide resources for certain species because their body may have certain requirements. Since different animals live in different locations due to their climate, a place that is always warm would be a habitat to animals and organisms that only live in warm places. I want to see a diverse range of species of animals and other organisms in the place I live. 

Lastly, constant heat from warm weather can cause health issues. I believe that prolonged heat exposure can cause many health issues such as dehydration and skin cancer. In a place that is always warm, the human body will sweat a lot as the heat in the body creates an exothermic reaction. This will cause the body to constantly need water in order to stay hydrated. Additionally, a place that is warm usually lacks water and is in a drought. With limited water supply and a high chance of dehydration, the human body will have nutrient deficiencies and would not remain healthy in a warm place.

In conclusion, I would not live in a place that is constantly warm because of the lack of experience in different climates, health concerns it would cause, and the inadequate diversity in the ecosystem. The warm weather would only let me enjoy the warmth of nature and I would be lacking enjoyment of other seasons. In addition, I would want my body to remain healthy in a place that I have to live in. I would be happy living in a place that is warm temporarily. Although, I would not enjoy staying in a place that is always warm.

task_prompt: Would you live in a place that is always warm?
response_text:
There are many warm places in the world; many parts of Africa and Southeast Asia are very warm for the majority of the year. Having lived in Hong Kong, a part of Asia, for many years of my life, I can confidently state that I would not choose to live in a place that is constantly warm. This can be attributed to the climate of said place, the constant humid weather, and the abundance of bugs and pests. 

First of all, there would be little to no variation in temperatures if a place was warm. This could mean that it would constantly be hot, even throughout the winter months. When there are very hot days, especially in the summer, a fan or the air conditioner (AC) would be necessary in order to prevent heat-related diseases like heatstroke. If everyone living in this warm place needed to turn on the AC or the fan, it could greatly damage the environment, since both the AC and fan will require a lot of energy and electricity to run all throughout the year. There is already an ongoing problem with our demand for more electricity, and the over-consumption of energy, that I personally do not want to contribute to if I do not have to. 

In addition, a constantly warm place would not have snow or hail, meaning that precipitation would be transmitted through rain. The weather would be constantly damp and humid, something that I would not enjoy every day if I were to live in this place. My body would produce a lot of sweat while living in a damp and warm place, which leaves a sticky feeling on a person's skin -- a feeling that I do not particularly enjoy. If it was winter, I would much rather have snow or hail because I love the sight of the stereotypical "North American winter," one with an abundance of snow which would properly indicate that winter has truly come. 

Lastly, I would have a problem with the pests or bugs. In a place that is constantly warm, such as Asia or Africa, having a large amount of bugs like mosquitos and flies are quite common. As a person who reacts very badly to bug bites, this may prove to be a challenge for me, as many of these bugs enter homes and are pretty unavoidable. To add on, many warm places have pests that are able to transmit diseases, such as malaria, which could be a great risk to anyone's health, and must be consider before moving to a constantly warm place. 

To conclude, I would not live in a place where it is constantly warm due to the fact that the climate, weather and pests that this place brings with living there could affect the environment, my personal health and well-being. Though it may be nice to visit a warm location like Asia once in a while as a vacation, I have fully adjusted to living in the environment of Canada.

Although issues such as FOMO (fear of missing out) and spending hours every day scrolling are important, the real problem comes in when the aftereffects are explored. Studies have shown that the rapid-cycle viewing style of most social media platforms drastically heightens the stress and anxieties of the user. To balance a social life, academics, and an entire job would surely pressure and overwork anybody, especially a teenager. This three-tiered balancing act is not only unsustainable for youth, but also places them in a position where they are too busy to enjoy their childhood. The skyrocketing prices found in Canada are putting too much stress on families, leading teenagers to excessively busy themselves with employment.

It is an absolutely ridiculous expectation for children to manage a workload most adults could not, and this inevitably leads to teens being too busy. The unrealistic standards for post-secondary education leads teenagers to fill their time up with activities solely dedicated to improving their acceptance rates, and neglecting the other aspects of their lives.

To allow children to live in a society where they are constantly bombarded by social media, requiring jobs to live, and straining themselves to get a proper education is testament to the apathetic view held by many. task_prompt: Would you live in a place that is always warm?
response_text:
While people definitely have varying opinions on whether they would live somewhere that is warm all the time, I know that I personally would definitely not choose to live there. I have multiple reasons to back up my opinion, including:

My personal preferences
I don't like the feeling of being warm. I like the variety in Canadian temperatures. The summer is a time that I enjoy, but after a few weeks of constant heat, I begin to miss the cold Canadian winters. I also don't like the bugs outside, or the sweat, or the heavy, muggy, humid heat in the air. I also get sun burnt very easily, so constant sun is not a good option for me.

The fact that heat is dangerous
The sun is not something that is always safe. Around 8.3 million people die every year due to heat exhaustion/stroke and around 15.7 million people die from sun cancer every year. As a lifeguard, I've seen symptoms of heat exhaustion/stroke up close, some of which include being sun burnt, constantly dehydrated, completely exhausted, becoming delirious/starting to hallucinate, losing control of limbs and more and it seems to me like a horrible way to die. Sun cancer symptoms are likely similar, although I haven't seen them up close, but they could be even worse.

The logistics of the idea
If a place is constantly warm, with no rain for example, it would not have a very healthy environment, and I wonder how the community would do well in such an area. I assume they would have difficulty accessing simple things, like water and their self grown food, so the community would be completely dependent on others for their survival and wellbeing. I consider myself an independent person, and being completely dependent on others for my basic survival needs is not something I would do willingly.

Canadian weather and my experiences
In Canada, it does get hot in the summer, but we don't feel it all year round and even in the summer, we still have lots of varying weather. Sometimes it's 20 degrees outside, then the next day it's 40, then the next day it's pouring rain and 10 degrees. I've never been in a climate where it's fully warm all the time. Even on vacations to Mexico, Miami, and even Jamaica, I've never been in a place where it's been completely warm for more than around 5 days straight. I'm not accustomed to it.

I can see why people would say yes, if they like warmth,  if they already live in a warm climate, if they live in a consistently cold climate and want to find somewhere different, etc. but I would not willingly live somewhere that is warm all the time. In contrast, I also definitely would not live somewhere that is cold all the time, but talking about warm climates, I don't thrive in them, the heat makes me crazy sometimes and I just know it would not be a good option for me.

Climate change can cause sudden and dramatic changes to the weather and climate of the planet, including more frequent natural disasters. 

One way it affects humans is flooding. People who live in seaside cities and islands are affected the most by this. Rising global temperatures cause sea ice to melt, this adds more water into the ocean, causing sea levels to rise, causing the flooding. Oceans rise steadily and encroach further into land, flooding buildings and homes. This also affects seaside animals. Creatures like sea turtles who lay eggs on beaches to hatch, run the risk of having their eggs or babies swept up by the tides and being injured or killed.

For example, polar bears who depend on the ice for hunting during the winter months are now seeing a decrease in population due to starvation. This is not an independent case, many animals like the polar bears are nearing eradication due to climate change. 

On the opposite end of the spectrum, people in dryer climates (like our prairies here in Canada) have noticed an increase in deadly forest fires which can affect biodiversity in nature and pose a heavy risk to life and property. Climate change has caused the ozone layer in our atmosphere to weaken, causing the sun's rays to more easily pass through. In dry areas, that heavily concentrated sun, on already dry land, can easily set ablaze. This burns many plants before they have the chance to pollinate and reproduce.

They take in the carbon dioxide we exhale and transform it into oxygen (via photosynthesis) which we breathe in. So to support ourselves we need to ensure we are properly supporting our ecosystems.

The want or need  for financial independence pushes teens to go out and get a job. Working often takes up what little spare time teens would have. Also, extracurricular activities such as sports, music, arts, or community play take a crucial part in shaping teenagers personal and social development. While thesenactivities offer valuable opportunitues for growth and self discovery, they also demand a significant time investment. whether it's attending practices, rehearsals, or volunteering events, teenagers often find themselves streched thin as they try to juggle many different things. 

Nother reason why today's teenagers are very busy is because of family obligations. From household chores and responsibilities, teens are often expected to contribute to the functioning of thier housholds. wether it's helping with childcare, running errands, or assisting elderly family members, these duties can take up a big amount of time and energy. This leaves today's teens with very little spare time. 

Lastly, societal and peer pressure play a huge role in teenagers schedules. The fear of missing out drives many teens to overcommit themselves in an attempt to keep up with there peers. Wether it's attending social events, joining clubs, or participating in recreational activities, teenagers often feel compelled to pack their scheduled to avoid feeling left out. 

In conclusion, the busyness of teenagers is driven by many different and changing factors. task_prompt: Are today's teen too busy?
response_text:
The teens of Canada today are not too busy. The workload that they are responsible for is a reasonable amount, and could even be considered less than needed. While it is true that students may experience high amounts of stress, it is not a daily matter and often happens as a result of the student themself choosing to partake in extracurricular activities or working part/full-time. 

Firstly, the time teens in Canada spend at school is below most of the other countries, with six hours and thirty minutes. Although I am not criticising this decision, this undoubtably allows Canadian teens to be less busy. For example, the United States has school days that last 8 hours, and South Korea has days which last over 10 hours. The reduced time spent in school allows for the average Canadian teenager to balance out their education with life and extracurriculars. It also gives them more free time, as they can complete their homework and assignments earlier than their counterparts in other nations. The lessened amount of time spent at school ensures that teenagers in Canada are not too busy. 

Additionally, the amount and difficulty of homework, tests, and assignments that are given to be completed outside of school is feasible. Canadian teenagers at this level are given only a few assignments on average per week. In most of my classes, the students are given assignments which can completed quickly, and have plenty of free time remaining. I can attest to this as I am a student, and I only spend about an hour a day on homework/studies and two or three hours on extracurriculars. It is also common to hear in my classroom that tests and projects are referred to as easy and simple. Thus, with wise time management, students in Canada can get a lot done during the day while still having space and time for hobbies.

Lastly, I am a student that has been enrolled in both the Chinese and Canadian education system, and I would say that by experience and by witness, the Canadian system is far easier. For comparison, it is common in China and other countries for students to spend the majority of their twenty-four hours completing schoolwork and balancing it with extracurriculars. In contrast, Canadian teens spend only about a quarter of their day in learning environments.

In conclusion, I do not believe that teens in Canada are too busy. Firstly, their reduced time spent in schools, which allows for them to balance out their school and life easier. Secondly, the difficulty and amount of assignments is relatively low, with most being able to complete their work using only a few hours. Lastly, the Canadian school system is, by contrast, far easier than the schools of most other countries, and makes the teens and students of Canada less busy.
